question.prompt: What is the hundreds digit of \(2011^{2011}?\)

solutions.explanation:
The hundreds digit is determined by the last three digits. Replacing a factor by an integer differing by a multiple of \(1000\) does not change the last three digits of a product. Thus we may replace the base \(2011\) by \(11=1+10\).

Consider multiplying \(2011\) factors of \(1+10\). In the expansion, any term choosing \(10\) from at least three factors is divisible by \(1000\), so it cannot affect the last three digits. We need only the terms choosing zero, one, or two tens.

There is one way to choose no tens and \(2011\) ways to choose one ten. There are \(2011\cdot2010/2\) ways to choose two tens: choosing the two factors in order counts each pair twice. Every expanded term belongs to exactly one of these cases or to the discarded case of at least three tens. Therefore, for some integer \(K\),
\[
11^{2011}=1+2011\cdot10+\frac{2011\cdot2010}{2}\cdot100+1000K.
\]
The three retained contributions add to
\[
1+20{,}110+202{,}105{,}500=202{,}125{,}611.
\]
Consequently, \(2011^{2011}\) ends in \(611\). Its hundreds digit is \(\boxed{6}\), choice D.
solutions.title: Keep the terms that affect the last three digits

solutions.explanation:
We need only the remainder after division by \(1000\), because it gives the last three digits. Write \(u\equiv v\pmod{1000}\) when \(u-v\) is divisible by \(1000\). Such replacements preserve remainders in products, so
\[
2011^{2011}\equiv11^{2011}\pmod{1000}.
\]
To shorten the exponent, look for a power of \(11\) whose remainder is \(1\). First,
\[
11^5=161{,}051\equiv51\pmod{1000}.
\]
Successive squaring gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
11^{10}&\equiv51^2\equiv601,\\
11^{20}&\equiv601^2\equiv201,\\
11^{40}&\equiv201^2\equiv401
\end{aligned}
\qquad\pmod{1000}.
\]
Hence
\[
11^{50}\equiv401\cdot601=241{,}001\equiv1\pmod{1000}.
\]
Multiplying by \(11^{50}\) therefore leaves the remainder unchanged. Since \(2011=40\cdot50+11\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
11^{2011}&=(11^{50})^{40}11^{11}\\
&\equiv601\cdot11\equiv611\pmod{1000}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last three digits are \(611\), so the hundreds digit is \(\boxed{6}\), choice D.
